title: Why Do We Compare Our Relationships to Other People's?
metaTitle: Why We Compare Our Relationships to Others'
metaDescription: We compare relationships for the same reasons we compare everything else — but against a curated highlight reel. Here is what the research suggests.
keyFinding: Comparing your relationship to other people's is a normal extension of ordinary social comparison, but it tends to mislead because you are measuring your full reality against other people's edited best moments, and research links this kind of comparison to lower relationship satisfaction.
honestAnswer: We compare our relationships to other people's for the same reason we compare almost everything — it is how humans gauge where they stand when there is no objective measure. Leon Festinger's social comparison theory describes this as a built-in process: lacking an absolute standard for 'is my relationship good?', we reach for other couples as the yardstick. Relationships are simply one more domain that comparison sweeps up.

What makes relationship comparison especially distorting is what we actually get to see. The version of other people's relationships on display — particularly on social media — is a curated highlight reel of affection, anniversaries, and milestones, with none of the ordinary friction every couple has. So we end up comparing our own behind-the-scenes, frustrations and dull stretches included, against everyone else's edited best moments. Research links this social-media relationship comparison to lower relationship satisfaction and more jealousy, which is the predictable result of an uneven comparison.
whatDataShows: Festinger's 1954 social comparison theory holds that people evaluate themselves by comparison with others, especially where objective standards are missing — and the quality of a relationship has almost no objective yardstick. That makes relationships a natural target for comparison: we infer how ours is doing partly by looking at how others' appear to be doing.

The input is heavily skewed. What we observe of other couples, and above all what appears on social media, is selectively positive — public displays of affection, celebrations, and milestones, rather than the disagreements, boredom, and repair work that are ordinary parts of a relationship. We are, in effect, comparing our complete, unfiltered experience to other people's curated presentation.

Research on social media and relationships suggests this comparison carries a cost. Studies in this area link comparing one's relationship to others' online with lower relationship satisfaction and with more jealousy. The mechanism is straightforward: when the comparison standard is an idealised highlight reel, an ordinary, healthy relationship can look deficient against it, even though nothing about the relationship has actually changed.
whyItFeelsDifferent: The comparison feels valid because the highlight reel looks like the whole picture. You do not see the other couple's tense silences or unglamorous routines, so the curated fragments read as a faithful summary of their life together. Comparing your full reality to that edited version feels like comparing like with like, when it is anything but.

It also feels different because relationships are private from the inside and performed from the outside. You experience your own relationship in all its ordinary texture, while you experience others' mostly through what they choose to show. That asymmetry — inside knowledge of your own, surface knowledge of theirs — reliably tilts the comparison against your own relationship.

And the friction that every couple has tends to be invisible precisely because it is normal and unremarkable. People rarely post the dull evening or the unresolved argument, so the baseline ordinary parts of a relationship disappear from view entirely. The result is a sense that other couples are not just happier but somehow frictionless, a standard that no real relationship meets — including the ones on the other side of the screen.
whatResearchSaysToDo: The most consistent implication is to correct the comparison set rather than try to win the comparison. Recognising that what you see of others is a curated slice — and that the ordinary friction missing from it is present in every relationship, including theirs — tends to take the air out of the comparison without anything about your relationship needing to change.

Reducing exposure to the most curated, upward-comparison-heavy input also fits the research. Because the link between social-media relationship comparison and lower satisfaction is concentrated where people consume the most idealised content, cutting back on that input is a direct way to reduce a distorted self-assessment. The aim is a less skewed picture, not more effort to match an unreal standard.

Shifting from comparing against other couples toward attending to your own relationship is the other direction the evidence points. Evaluating a relationship on its own terms — what is actually working and not working between the two of you — sidesteps the highlight-reel distortion entirely, because the curated lives of strangers were never a meaningful benchmark for your particular relationship in the first place.
whatDoesNotHelp: Trying to out-perform the highlight reel — staging your own relationship to look as good as the ones you envy — does not address the distortion; it just adds you to it. It also tends to widen the gap for everyone, since each curated display raises the standard others measure themselves against, which is the same dynamic that made you feel worse.

Reading curated posts as accurate data about other couples does not help, because the input is selectively positive by construction. Treating a highlight reel as a full account leads to a confidently wrong conclusion: that other relationships lack the ordinary friction yours has, when in reality that friction is simply edited out of view.

Generic reassurance that 'every relationship is great in its own way' tends to be thin, because it does not engage the actual source of the feeling. The research points to a specific, correctable distortion — full reality versus edited best moments — and addressing that mechanism directly tends to do more than vague positive framing that the comparison was never really about.
realNumbersInContext: This is a domain where the honest picture is structural rather than a single statistic, and the specific figures from social-media studies vary by sample and method — so treat any precise number with caution. The well-supported pattern is the direction of the effect: research links comparing your relationship to others' on social media with lower relationship satisfaction and more jealousy, and the mechanism is the mismatch between your full reality and others' curated presentation.

The number worth keeping in mind is closer to none — the share of relationships that are actually free of the ordinary friction a highlight reel omits. Against that, the useful context is not how your relationship ranks against the curated lives you see, but that those lives are edited and the friction missing from them is universal. Comparing relationships is normal; the reason it misleads is that you are measuring your behind-the-scenes against everyone else's best moments.

faqs.question: Why do I compare my relationship to other couples?
faqs.answer: Because comparison is how humans gauge where they stand when there is no objective standard — and 'is my relationship good?' has almost none. Festinger's social comparison theory describes this as a built-in process, and relationships are simply one more domain it sweeps up.

faqs.question: Does comparing my relationship to others actually harm it?
faqs.answer: Research on social media and relationships links comparing your relationship to others' online with lower relationship satisfaction and more jealousy. The likely reason is that the comparison is uneven: you measure your full reality against other couples' curated, selectively positive presentation.

faqs.question: Why do other people's relationships look so much better online?
faqs.answer: Because what gets shown is a highlight reel — affection, celebrations, and milestones — while the disagreements, boredom, and ordinary friction are edited out. You are seeing other couples' best moments and comparing them against your own behind-the-scenes, which includes everything.

faqs.question: How do I stop comparing my relationship to others'?
faqs.answer: The research points to correcting the comparison rather than winning it: recognising that what you see of others is curated and that the ordinary friction missing from it exists in every relationship. Reducing exposure to idealised content and evaluating your relationship on its own terms tend to help more than trying to match an unreal standard.

faqs.question: Is it normal to feel jealous when I see other couples?
faqs.answer: Yes — it is a common response, and research links relationship comparison on social media with more jealousy. It does not necessarily say anything is wrong with your relationship; more often it reflects the distortion of comparing your full reality to someone else's edited best moments.

dataSources: Festinger, L. (1954). A Theory of Social Comparison Processes. Human Relations, 7(2), 117–140.
Research on social media use and romantic relationships, linking online relationship comparison with lower relationship satisfaction and increased jealousy.
The 'highlight reel' distortion — the observation that what people present, especially on social media, is a curated, selectively positive slice rather than their full, ordinary reality.
